Hierarchical reinforcement learning for dynamic collision avoidance of 
autonomous ships under uncertain scenarios
Sijin Yu, Yunbo Li∗, Jiaye Gong
College of Ocean Science and Engineering, Shanghai Maritime University, Shanghai, China
a r t i c l e  i n f o
Keywords:
Autonomous ships
Dynamic collision avoidance
Hierarchical reinforcement learning
Uncertainty scenario
Maritime intelligent navigation
 
a b s t r a c t
Autonomous ships hold substantial potential for enhancing navigational safety, improving collision avoidance 
eﬃciency, and increasing adaptability in complex maritime environments, thereby presenting broad prospects 
for intelligent shipping. This paper introduces a dynamic collision avoidance control method based on a hierar-
chical reinforcement learning framework for autonomous ships. By integrating high-level global intent planning 
with low-level ﬁne-grained rudder control, the proposed approach markedly enhances the interpretability, sta-
bility, and behavioral consistency of the learned policy. Furthermore, a multidimensional uncertainty modeling 
mechanism is incorporated during training, systematically accounting for variations in initial states and obstacle 
behavior patterns, which eﬀectively strengthens policy adaptability and generalization under uncertain condi-
tions. To validate the method, simulations are conducted in representative encounter scenarios as well as in 
omnidirectional dynamic obstacle tests. A comprehensive evaluation is carried out using multiple control per-
formance metrics, environmental adaptability analysis, policy consistency assessment, and equivalent energy 
consumption comparisons. The results conﬁrm that the proposed approach achieves stable and reliable intelli-
gent collision avoidance control in highly dynamic environments, oﬀering a feasible and scalable solution for 
high-performance collision avoidance in intelligent maritime navigation.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Over the past decades, intelligent ships have gradually become a core technology in maritime transportation and surface operations, driven by continuous advancements in autonomous navigation and environmental perception [ 1 ]. In complex and highly dynamic maritime environments, autonomous collision avoidance capability has become a critical factor for ensuring navigational safety, particularly in scenarios characterized by frequent encounters with dynamic obstacles [ 2 ]. Consequently, dy- namic obstacle avoidance for ships has evolved into a highly active and widely studied research area [ 3 ]. As a powerful paradigm for sequential decision-making and optimal control, reinforcement learning (RL) has been increasingly applied to ship collision avoidance tasks [ 4 ]. Never- theless, achieving stable and efficient training of RL agents in dynamic environments with high uncertainty remains a major challenge in intel- ligent ship research. Inspired by biological learning mechanisms in nature, RL has been widely regarded as a promising intelligent decision-making paradigm for autonomous ship collision avoidance problems [ 5 ]. Collision avoid- ance in maritime navigation is inherently an environment-driven and dynamic response process, frequently encountered in practical shipping ∗ Corresponding author. E-mail address: yunboli630@gmail.com (Y. Li). and offshore operations, where decision-making requires real-time en- vironmental perception and continuous control of ship maneuvers [ 6 ]. Compared with conventional methods based on manually designed rules or physical modeling, RL offers distinct advantages, such as obviat- ing the need for precise system modeling and enabling adaptive policy learning through interaction with the environment. In recent years, RL has demonstrated notable adaptability and optimization capability in in- telligent ship collision avoidance control [ 7 ]. However, as task complex- ity increases and the motion patterns of dynamic obstacles become more diverse, striking a balance between training stability and policy gener- alization has become increasingly challenging [ 8 ]. Despite substantial progress in this area, developing robust, scalable, and highly generaliz- able RL-based collision avoidance algorithms under uncertain training scenarios remains a critical challenge for autonomous ship navigation research, particularly in light of the modeling complexities introduced by dynamic obstacle variations in real-world maritime environments. In recent years, deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has emerged as a core methodology for solving complex decision-making problems across diverse domains. sections.text: reinforcement learning algorithm for collision avoidance under uncertain scenarios 3.1. Hierarchical reinforcement learning architecture This study proposes a hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) framework [ 20 ]. By introducing a hierarchical structure, HRL decom- poses complex, long-horizon tasks into multiple sub-tasks at different levels of abstraction. In this framework, the high-level policy makes low-frequency decisions on global actions or sub-goals. In contrast, the low-level policy executes fine-grained control under the guidance of the high-level instructions. The HRL architecture adopted in this study is illustrated in Fig. 7 . The framework consists of two reinforcement learning agents: a high- level PPO agent responsible for global decision-making, and a low-level TD3 agent that executes fine-grained rudder adjustments. These two agents operate in a coordinated manner through state-space augmen- tation and residual control mechanisms, thereby enabling more precise control performance. The detailed algorithmic procedure is presented in Algorithm 1 .

The high- level agent outputs decisions every 𝑇 steps and updates its policy ev- ery 𝑚𝑇 steps, ensuring the stability of global decision-making. These mod- ifications are designed to improve the stability, sample efficiency, and exploration capability of the high-level agent. State space design The state space of the high-level agent is designed to provide a macro-level representation of the global environment, thereby support- ing the generation of coarse-grained rudder commands. The state input primarily consists of the own ship’s state variables ( 𝑥, 𝑦, 𝜓 ) , the distance to the target point 𝑑 target , the relative position of the obstacle ship with respect to the own ship ( 𝑥 rel , 𝑦 rel ) , the inter-ship distance 𝐷 , and the CRI. It provides the high-level policy with effective awareness of overall navi- gation trends, obstacle distribution, and potential collision risks, thereby facilitating the development of collision avoidance and steering strate- gies at a global level. The state space of the low-level agent is designed to emphasize sensi- tivity to local dynamic information and responsiveness to the high-level policy. In this study, the low-level local state is concatenated with the one-hot encoding of the high-level action, onehot ( 𝑎 𝐻 𝑡 ) ∈{0 , 1} 7 , yielding the following definition of the low-level state: ̃𝑠 𝐿 𝑡 = [ 𝑠 local , onehot ( 𝑎 𝐻 𝑡 ) ] = [ 𝑠 𝐻 𝑡 , 𝑣 rel , 𝜓 rel , onehot ( 𝑎 𝐻 𝑡 ) ] (30) This state vector not only preserves awareness of environmental and dynamic risk factors but also embeds high-level policy signals. This en- ables the low-level agent to fully interpret the high-level intent when generating continuous control actions, thereby ensuring consistency and fine-grained control in the action-output process. Action space design The action spaces of the high-level and low-level agents differ sig- nificantly in terms of representation, control granularity, and optimiza- tion objectives. The high-level agent takes the environmental state in- formation as input and outputs a coarse-grained rudder command. In this study, the high-level action space is designed as a discrete set of seven fixed rudder angles:  𝐻 = { −35 ◦ , −23 . 3 ◦ , −11 . 7 ◦ , 0 ◦ , +11 . 7 ◦ , +23 . 3 ◦ , +35 ◦ } (31) The low-level action space is defined as a bounded one-dimensional continuous space, which outputs a rudder residual 𝛿 res ∈ ℝ . The final control rudder angle is given by: 𝛿 final =  ( 𝛿 high , 𝛿 res ) = 𝛿 high + 𝜅 ⋅ 𝛿 res , 𝛿 res ∈[− ̄ 𝛿 max , ̄ 𝛿 max ] , (32) where ̄ 𝛿 max is the preset residual amplitude limit, and 𝜅 is a residual scaling factor that regulates the effective magnitude of low-level cor- rections. Since the low-level residual is always strictly constrained by 𝜅 ̄ 𝛿 max , and the final rudder angle 𝛿 final still satisfies the physical bound [ − 𝛿 max , 𝛿 max ] , the overall performance of the method is only mildly sen- sitive to the choice of 𝜅 . Experimental results demonstrate that within a reasonable range of 𝜅 ∈[0 . 8 , 1 . 2] , the proposed method exhibits stable performance, with variations mainly reflecting a trade-off between effi- ciency and control smoothness, rather than catastrophic degradation. In summary, by combining discrete and continuous action spaces, the high-level agent is responsible for global decision-making, while the low-level agent performs fine-grained corrections within a strictly con- trolled amplitude. This hierarchical design enables the policy to main- tain both convergence stability and strong adaptability in complex and dynamic scenarios. 4.3. sections.heading: Results
sections.text: and analysis This section aims to comprehensively analyze the performance of the proposed hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) strategy for dy- namic ship collision avoidance from three perspectives: the training process, collision avoidance performance, and representative scenario behaviors. To highlight the performance advantages introduced by the hierarchical design, three baselines are considered for comparison: (1) the classical single-layer reinforcement learning algorithm, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) [ 39 ]; (2) an RL-Rule hybrid method [ 40 ], in which heuristic decisions derived from the COLREGs are incorporated into the reinforcement learning policy to enhance compliance; and (3) the proposed hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL). Four represen- tative collision avoidance scenarios are designed for evaluation, namely head-on, crossing from the port side, crossing from the starboard side, and overtaking, which together cover the most common dynamic en- counter situations defined by COLREGs. 5.1. Comparative analysis of reward functions To evaluate the learning efficiency and policy stability of the pro- posed HRL strategy during training, a comparative analysis is conducted against the traditional PPO algorithm and the PPO-Rule hybrid method across four representative collision avoidance scenarios. Fig. 11 illus- trates the reward function trends of the three methods throughout the training process, where the horizontal axis denotes the training steps and the vertical axis represents the corresponding cumulative reward. All curves are smoothed using a moving average, and the shaded areas indicate the standard deviation range, thereby reflecting the stability of each algorithm during training. As shown in Fig. 11 , in the head-on and overtaking scenarios, the HRL strategy is able to quickly achieve higher rewards in the early stages of training and maintain stable convergence, ultimately reaching a re- ward level significantly superior to the baseline methods. In contrast, PPO converges more slowly in these scenarios and exhibits pronounced fluctuations during training. Benefiting from rule-based guidance, PPO- Rule achieves faster convergence than plain PPO; however, its final re- ward level and stability remain inferior to HRL. In the crossing from port side scenario, PPO can obtain slightly higher final rewards after long-term training. Nevertheless, HRL rapidly attains a high reward level in the early phase and maintains a smoother improvement trend throughout the process, reflecting stronger learn- ing efficiency and stability. The performance of PPO-Rule lies in be- tween: its training fluctuations are relatively small, but the final reward level is still lower than that of HRL. In the crossing-from-starboard sce- nario, the three methods achieve comparable final rewards overall. HRL again demonstrates smoother improvement during the middle and early phases, while PPO-Rule, aided by rule guidance, shows reduced variance but consistently lower reward values compared with HRL. Overall, HRL achieves higher final rewards in most representative scenarios and exhibits faster convergence across all cases. Although in the port-and-starboard-crossing encounters, its training stability is slightly inferior to PPO-Rule, HRL consistently demonstrates clear ad- vantages in both convergence speed and final reward performance. These results highlight the superior robustness and generalization ability of HRL under uncertain environments. Meanwhile, PPO-Rule alleviates to some extent the training instability of PPO, but its overall perfor- mance improvements remain limited. Furthermore, to further validate the performance improvement of the proposed strategy, the arrival rate and avoidance success rate across different scenarios were recorded during training, as summarized in Table 4 . sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: This study proposed a hierarchical reinforcement learning-based dy- namic collision avoidance strategy for autonomous ships navigating in complex and uncertain environments. The framework decouples high- level global decision-making from low-level rudder control, enabling the agent to effectively address frequent obstacle variations and uncertain- ties in initial conditions. Comparative experiments in four representative COLREGs encounter scenarios demonstrate that HRL consistently outperforms the conven- tional PPO and PPO-Rule baselines in terms of avoidance success rate, navigation efficiency, trajectory smoothness, and risk control. Further tests under omnidirectional dynamic obstacles confirm its strong gener- alization capability, while the introduction of energy-consumption met- rics shows that HRL achieves safer and more efficient maneuvers with re- duced rudder workload and trajectory deviations. Moreover, behavioral analysis indicates that the generated action sequences are interpretable and regulation-compliant, highlighting the framework’s engineering ap- plicability. In conclusion, the proposed HRL strategy effectively enhances both safety and efficiency in autonomous ship collision avoidance, offering a promising solution for practical deployment in highly dynamic mar- itime environments. Future work will focus on extending the framework to multi-ship cooperative avoidance, improving energy-efficient control, and conducting real-world validation on physical autonomous ship plat- forms to further bridge the gap between simulation and practice.
